paras: The attempted lynching of George Robinson took place in Frederick, Maryland, on the night of February 23, 1888, when an excited crowd tried to lynch a Black man who had just been arrested on an accusation of attempted assault at a hotel. Robinson was lodged in jail before the effort succeeded, and two days later he was bound over to the grand jury. The story ran briefly in white papers in Washington, Wilmington, Baltimore and Shepherdstown, under headlines that stressed the danger to the prisoner.

According to a dispatch from Frederick, Robinson, described as 'a negro of bad character', was accused of attempting to criminally assault Sallie Jackson in her room at the United States Hotel. Her screams were said to have prevented the assault, and Robinson was captured the same night.

As the Evening Star printed the dispatch, Robinson was 'lodged in jail before a desperate effort made to lynch him by an excited crowd was successful.' The Wilmington Daily Republican's version added that there were fears he would be taken from the jail and hanged before morning. No later report describes an attack on the jail, and a week afterward the Shepherdstown Register said only that 'Threats of lynching were made.'

On February 25 the Baltimore German-language daily Der Deutsche Correspondent reported that Robinson had been bound over by a judge to the grand jury, which was then in session. The same paper said he was also accused of indecent attacks on two women of Locust Alley, Mrs. Theodore Lowe and Mrs. George Green. No report of an indictment, trial or sentence appears in the coverage.

The white press treated the episode as a short item built on one wire dispatch, which the Evening Star headed 'A Frederick, Md., Negro in Danger of Lynching' and the Wilmington paper headed 'His Neck is in Danger.' Both versions called Robinson 'a negro of bad character' and stated the assault as fact rather than as a charge. Der Deutsche Correspondent covered only the court step and the further accusations, without mentioning the crowd, while the Shepherdstown Register reduced the story to a line among its 'Items of Interest' that named the race of both parties.

The Wilmington Daily Republican called the prisoner Charles Robinson, while the Baltimore and Shepherdstown papers gave his name as George. The Wilmington paper also called the accuser 'Miss' Sallie Jackson, where the Evening Star and the Baltimore paper called her 'Mrs.'

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Robinson
bases: A crowd tried to lynch Robinson after his arrest on an assault accusation and he was feared to be in danger of being taken from jail and hanged (A1, A2); no one was killed, so it is an attempted lynching.

An 'excited crowd' made 'a desperate effort' to lynch Robinson over an accusation of attempted assault, but he was lodged in jail and no killing is reported (A1, A2, A5); it was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The arrest and accusation appear in the Frederick wire dispatch (A1, A2), in an independently worded Baltimore German report (A4) and in a later brief (A5); the crowd's effort to lynch rests on the single wire dispatch (A1, A2), with A5 saying only that threats were made.

accounts.label: Frederick wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Robinson, 'a negro of bad character', tried to assault Sallie Jackson at the United States Hotel, was captured and jailed, and an excited crowd made a desperate but unsuccessful effort to lynch him; fears were felt that he would be taken from jail and hanged.

accounts.label: Baltimore German-language report
accounts.gist: George Robinson, arrested two days earlier for an indecent assault on Mrs. Sallie Jackson, was bound over to the grand jury and was said to have also attacked two other women; no mention of a mob.

accounts.label: Weekly news brief
accounts.gist: George Robinson, 'a colored man', was arrested for an attempted assault on a white woman, and threats of lynching were made.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed the dispatch 'A Frederick, Md., Negro in Danger of Lynching' and, like the wire, called him 'a negro of bad character', presenting the assault accusation as fact.
The Wilmington Daily Republican ran the same dispatch under 'His Neck is in Danger', stressing fears he would be hanged before morning.
Der Deutsche Correspondent reported only the court step and further accusations under 'Nachrichten aus Frederick', without mentioning the crowd.
The Shepherdstown Register reduced the story to one line among 'Items of Interest', naming the race of both parties and noting threats of lynching.

George Robinson (A4, A5), called Charles Robinson in A2; described as 'a negro of bad character' (A1, A2) and 'a colored man' (A5)

Accused of attempting to criminally assault Mrs. (or Miss) Sallie Jackson in her room at the United States Hotel; her screams were said to have prevented it. A4 adds reports that he had also made indecent attacks on Mrs. Theodore Lowe and Mrs. George Green of Locust Alley.
